content.content: Shout 'Man Overboard', press MOB on GPS if available, and maintain visual contact.

Throw flotation and a marker, then execute the preferred recovery maneuver for conditions.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Assign roles: spotter points continuously; helm controls speed and approach; crew prepares recovery gear.

sideA.content: What are the first three steps in a MOB event?

sideB.content: Raise the alarm and mark the position, throw flotation/marker, and keep constant visual while maneuvering for recovery.

content.content: Reduce speed and balance sails to stabilize course while troubleshooting.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Inspect linkage, quadrant, and cables; rig an emergency tiller if possible.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Use drogues, warps, or sail trim to maintain heading until repairs or refuge.

flashcards.title: FC: Loss of Steering: Tiller/Rudder Failure

sideA.content: How can you control heading after steering failure?

sideB.content: Balance sails, reduce speed, and use an emergency tiller or drag devices (drogue/warps).

content.content: Use PAN-PAN for urgent but not life-threatening help; SECURITÉ for safety broadcasts (e.g., hazards).
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
State vessel name/callsign, position, nature of problem, and intentions on VHF Ch. 16.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Shift to a working channel when directed; keep transmissions short and clear.

sideA.content: When do you use PAN-PAN vs SECURITÉ?

sideB.content: PAN-PAN is for urgent assistance; SECURITÉ is a safety broadcast about hazards or navigation warnings.

content.content: Shift to neutral immediately to minimize damage; avoid restarting until cleared.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
If conditions allow, heave-to or anchor; use a hook/knife on a pole or dive only with proper safety.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
After clearing, inspect for vibration, leaks, or steering issues before resuming passage.

flashcards.title: FC: Line in Prop / Fouled Propeller

sideA.content: Why should you avoid restarting after a foul?

sideB.content: Restarting can wrap tighter, damage the shaft, cutlass bearing, or transmission.

content.content: Triage loads: switch to essential circuits and check main fuses/breakers and battery switches.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Inspect for burning smells, hot wires, or loose connections; isolate the faulted branch.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Use backup nav/comm gear (handheld VHF, paper charts) and plan for charging or diversion.

sideA.content: What is your first step during sudden power loss?

sideB.content: Secure non-essentials and check main fuses/breakers and battery/bus connections.

content.content: Engine quits underway: Shift to neutral; hoist/trim sails to maintain control. Check fuel (valves, filters, water in separator), air (intake), and electrical (kill switch, battery, connections). If near a lee shore, prepare to **emergency anchor** early. Broadcast Sécurité/Pan-Pan as appropriate and troubleshoot systematically.

sideA.content: First steps when the engine dies underway?

sideB.content: Establish sail control, check fuel/air/electrical, prepare to emergency anchor if drifting toward hazards, and call for help as needed.

content.content: Torn sail or failed line/fitting: Head downwind to depower. Reef or drop the affected sail. Secure flogging cloth; use sail ties/tape. Consider a temporary **jury rig** (e.g., spare halyard as shroud, reef to reduce load). Avoid shock loads. Sail conservatively to safe harbor.

sideA.content: What do you do after a sail or rigging failure?

sideB.content: Head downwind to depower, secure/reef or drop the sail, jury-rig if safe, then sail conservatively to shelter.

content.content: Raise the alarm; all hands to stations. Identify type (electrical, fuel, galley). Shut down fuel/electrical sources if safe. Use appropriate **ABC extinguisher** with PASS (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep). Keep low, avoid smoke; prepare for abandon ship if uncontrollable. Make a Mayday if life/boat at risk.

sideA.content: How do you fight a boat fire safely?

sideB.content: Raise the alarm, shut down fuel/electrics, use an ABC extinguisher with PASS, avoid smoke, and issue a Mayday if the fire is uncontrolled.

content.content: Water ingress: Start all **bilge pumps**, assign a bailer. Find source (through-hull, shaft seal, hose, hull). Close seacocks; apply softwood plugs, clamps, tape, or collision mat. Lighten ship and head to nearest safe water. Call for help early (Pan-Pan/Mayday).

sideA.content: How do you respond to flooding?

sideB.content: Start bilge pumps, locate the leak, plug/secure it (plugs, clamps, mat), close seacocks, and call for help early.

content.content: Stop engine if sand/mud ingestion risk. Check hull/keel for damage and rising water. Note position/tide; attempt to float off with rising tide, heeling, or weight shift. Try **kedging**: carry anchor to deeper water and winch off. Call for assistance if needed.

sideB.content: Check for damage/flooding, assess tide, reduce loads, try heeling or kedging to deeper water, and seek assistance if needed.

content.content: Loss of propulsion/control near hazards: Drop anchor **early** to arrest drift. Pay out 5–7:1 scope (more in heavy weather), snub to set. Use chain leader if available. Monitor position; be ready to re-set or add a second anchor. Communicate with traffic on VHF.

sideA.content: When and how to perform an emergency anchoring?

sideB.content: Drop early before hazards, use 5–7:1 scope (more in heavy weather), snub to set, monitor position, and be ready to re-set or add a second anchor.

content.content: When a squall hits: Reef **before** you must. Steer a safe course to reduce heel and loads. Consider **heaving-to** or running off under control. Keep crew clipped in; close hatches; rig preventer carefully. Track lightning and avoid metal contact if nearby.

sideA.content: What are immediate actions in a sudden squall?

sideB.content: Reef early, steer to reduce loads, consider heaving-to or running off, clip in crew, secure hatches, and manage preventers carefully.

content.content: Ensure scene safety; don gloves. Conduct primary survey (Airway, Breathing, Circulation). Control bleeding, immobilize fractures, treat for shock. Call for medical advice/evac (VHF Ch16 / DSC). Log vitals and interventions; head to nearest port if needed.

sideA.content: First priorities in a medical emergency aboard?

sideB.content: Scene safety, ABCs, control bleeding, immobilize, treat for shock, call for medical help, and record vitals while heading to port if needed.
